note: Measured from the official Reading and Writing questions (2,030 items, by official difficulty) for structure only: lengths, question forms, what changes with difficulty. No question text. Ranges are passage words (not counting the question line) and average words per answer choice. 1 easy, 2 medium, 3 hard.
global: Hard passages are longer and denser than easy ones: longer sentences (about 25–33 words on average in hard grammar and evidence passages, against 18–23 in easy ones) and more long academic words.

In hard questions with sentence-length choices, the correct answer is usually NOT the longest choice (it is the longest in only about 1 hard question in 4). Make the wrong choices as long, specific and detailed as the right one.
Use the official question line for each type, word for word (listed under each type).

Boundaries.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
patterns: Easy questions are mostly about commas or no punctuation; hard ones mostly test semicolons, periods and colons between full clauses, inside long sentences with harmless inner commas and modifiers.

Form, structure, and sense.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
patterns: Hard choices are longer (several words, e.g. whole verb phrases or modifier-plus-subject) and the subject is far from the verb or the antecedent far from the pronoun.

Transitions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
patterns: Easy answers are common transitions (however, as a result, for example, next).

Hard answers are mostly less common ones: as such, to that end, that said, granted, alternatively, of course, accordingly, hence, what's more, that is, in fact, indeed, likewise, specifically. The relationship turns on a subtle point, often a concession or a restatement rather than a plain contrast.

Rhetorical synthesis.question: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
patterns: Notes are short bullet sentences. About a quarter of goals ask to contrast or compare; others ask to introduce, emphasize, explain or present to a specific audience.
In hard questions every choice is accurate to the notes; only one meets every part of the goal.

Central ideas and details.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?  (easy and medium only, sometimes: According to the text, what is true about ___?)
patterns: About 1 in 4 passages is literary (an excerpt from a novel, story or poem, introduced as 'The following text is from…').
Detail ('According to the text') questions are common at easy (about 40%) and nearly absent at hard: hard questions ask for the main idea.
In hard questions the correct choice is the longest only about 1 time in 6.

Command of evidence: textual.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?  |  Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?  |  …would most directly weaken the underlined claim?
patterns: Weaken questions are rare (none at easy, under 10% at hard).
Quotation questions give the claim plus a short introduction; the choices are lines or sentences from an original work, about 20–35 words at medium and hard.
Hard claims have several parts or a condition; the correct choice is the longest only about 1 time in 4.

Command of evidence: quantitative.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?  (also: …to support the researchers' conclusion? / …to complete the example? / …to complete the text?)
patterns: Hard choices are long, data-heavy sentences; at least two are accurate to the table. The correct choice is the longest only about 1 time in 3.
Tables have a title line and 2–4 data columns; hard tables include a column or row the claim doesn't need.

Inferences.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
patterns: Every question ends the passage with a blank: the choices complete its last sentence.
Hard passages chain several qualified steps; the correct choice is the longest only about 1 time in 4.

Words in context.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?  (sometimes, mostly at easy: As used in the text, what does the word "___" most nearly mean?)
patterns: Choice words get longer and rarer with difficulty: about 9–10 letters on average at easy, 11+ at hard (e.g. untenable, idiosyncratic, circumscribed).
About 1 in 4 medium and hard questions uses short phrases as choices.
Hard passages have long sentences (about 30 words) and the clue is often a restatement or a concession, not a plain contrast word.

Text structure and purpose.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?  |  Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?  |  Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence (or portion) in the text as a whole?
patterns: About 30% of passages are literary.
About 40–50% are underlined-function questions; the rest split between main purpose and overall structure.

Cross-text connections.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?  |  Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
patterns: Both texts together run about 120–150 words, at every difficulty.
Some questions ask what both authors would agree with. At hard, about 1 in 10 asks how Text 1's author would respond to Text 2.
